body_markdown:
When talking about famous racing brands, Jaguar isn’t typically at the top of the list. Not anymore, anyhow. Sure, it had more than a little success, but there have also been extended periods of time when Jaguar was more than happy to stick to the personal luxury for which it has become famous. One of places Jaguar got racing right, however, was at Le Mans, and one of the periods it excelled there came in the late 1980s. If you need proof, I’m happy to introduce the Jaguar XJR-9, which is still all-original from its time on track at the 1988 24 Hours of Le Mans—where it won outright.


This drive comes courtesy of[Ben Collins Drives on YouTube](https://youtu.be/sN6UoO3qg4Q?si=xEdcYr48DOeNwcj_) , who somehow got access to the car straight out of museum storage. The XJR-9 is still in all-original condition, though it appears to have been at least cleaned up, unlike some other race cars we’ve seen that went from the victory circle straight to the display stand.


The XJR-9 was the result of Jaguar taking a renewed fancy to motorsport in the 1980s, beginning with the XJS racing in the European Touring Car Championship. It was[Tom Walkinshaw Racing](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/tom-walkinshaw-left-a-lasting-legacy-in-international-motorsports/) that put the XJS on the podium of ETCC and became the natural source to develop the XJR-9 and field it in Group C competition. Powered by a 7.0-liter V-12 making 700 horsepower, the XJR-9 was like the rest of the Group C field: powerful, slick, and incredibly fast.


The XJR-9 was significantly shorter than other Group C cars, because it was developed using a rolling road wind tunnel. The knowledge learned in the wind tunnel created the shape, but then that shape was constructed using the latest carbon fiber technology, where the entire monocoque was carbon and thus significantly stiffer than other cars on the starting line. The engine was naturally aspirated but likely weighed the same as turbocharged units due to the sheer size. Even with the massive engine shoved as far forward as possible, it was still a large mass relatively high in the chassis and came to define the car’s handling characteristics.

On track, Collins calls out that the driver’s view is basically just track and sky, relatively unobstructed. He points out that in most simulators the A-pillars blocked some vision, but in the real thing that was not even remotely a problem. The gearing is still Le Mans spec like everything else on the car, and that means Collins is struggling to manage the Jag on a smaller track. The steering is heavy in tight corners, as much of the geometry is set to be stable while pushing 240 mph on the Mulsanne Straight. It only takes a small throttle lift and a yank of the very tight shifter to grab a different gear and reset the revs for another pull through the range as you hear that big V-12 howl. Even on a tight track, with woefully out-of-date gear and the need to be careful as to not wad up a piece of history, piloting the Jag in its famous Silk Cut livery appears to be an experience for the ages.
